source.title: Mapping Overlaps in Benchmarks through Perplexity in the Wild
source.authors: Si-Yang Wu; Hong-Lin Bao; Si-Da Li; Ari Holtzman; James A. Evans

record.file_problem: Whole paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether token-level perplexity patterns predict benchmark performance, using regression and held-out prediction rather than the scaling sweeps in the original works.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results linking in-the-wild token perplexity features to benchmark performance, so those predictive results are recorded for V6. It does not test loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute, compute-optimal allocation, architecture-shape effects, other modalities, or scaling-law fit exponents. Results about benchmark overlap, semantic similarity, and benchmark categories are outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study is about benchmark overlap. It assumes that perplexity on in-the-wild text tracks benchmark performance, citing Thrush et al. and Hoffmann et al., and uses this as a tool to mine 'signatures': about 30 tokens per benchmark, forward-selected from about 1.7e7 candidates across 32 heterogeneous models. Its predictive numbers rate its own selected-feature regression: in-sample adjusted R² used to pick the granularity, plus LOOCV and held-out-model MAE as robustness checks. None of these measures whether downstream performance tracks scale or aggregate held-out pretraining loss, as V6 names. No version is tested, so these findings go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but misplaced in emphasis. The authors' main conclusion is that benchmark signatures (predictive token perplexities) reveal benchmark overlap structure that semantic similarity and performance correlations miss. They also find signatures robust to question-format confounds, overlap among knowledge and reasoning benchmarks, coding as the most isolated function, and low overlap among culture and humanities benchmarks. Predicting benchmark performance is a means to that end, not their conclusion about scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses token-level perplexity features from in-the-wild corpora, feature selection, and benchmark-performance regression rather than language-model size/data/compute scaling sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive fit varies with perplexity granularity and benchmark in Table 1. The paper also reports sensitivity analyses for screening ratio, feature selection method, and corpus choice, primarily on signature-structure outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexities on about 30 forward-selected RedPajama tokens predict benchmark scores across 32 mixed LLMs. LOOCV MAE on 27 BBH subtasks is 0.076±0.038, against 0.181±0.144 for a mean baseline. Held-out Qwen2.5-7B and Falcon-rw-7b give MAE 0.068 and 0.072.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse sets of token-level perplexities on in-the-wild corpora predict LLM benchmark performance across heterogeneous models.

fits_no_version.finding: In-sample adjusted R² of the selected-feature regressions varies by benchmark and granularity. It is high for GSM8K and MBPP (0.67–0.93) and lower for MMLU and TruthfulQA (0.19–0.55); doc-level is lowest.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well corpus perplexity predicts benchmarks depends on the benchmark and the perplexity granularity.

fits_no_version.finding: One BBH task's signature predicts another task's score worse than the mean baseline. Cross-task MAE is 0.223, against 0.021 task-specific and 0.181 for the mean.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perplexity-derived benchmark predictors are task-specific rather than a general capability factor.

record.problems: The predictive tests use cross-model associations and regression, not interventions or direct scaling sweeps. The main experiments use 32 models; the paper itself notes that token-level perplexity signatures are selected from a very high-dimensional feature space and describes possible screening limitations. Some reported adjusted R² values are modest.
record.rows_left_out: Benchmark signature-overlap matrices, semantic similarity results, within-category comparisons, and robustness statistics for corpus/method/threshold choices were left out because they do not measure a claim version's scaling-law or downstream-prediction outcome.

untested.parts: No relation of downstream performance to model scale or to aggregate held-out pretraining loss. Only the selected-token-perplexity predictor is evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked r1–r15 to V6. They are reassigned to none: the predictors are thousands-to-one selected token perplexities, not aggregate held-out loss or scale. Table 1 R² values are selection values used to justify the token granularity. The 32 models mix base and instruct models and families, with no scale analysis.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling of held-out pretraining loss with parameter count, tokens, or compute is tested.
No small-run power-law fits or predictions of larger-run loss are tested.
No fixed-compute allocation between model size and training tokens is tested.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count is tested.
No power-law tests in other modalities or training regimes are conducted.

The study tests whether selected in-the-wild token-perplexity features predict benchmark performance across models. It does not test whether downstream performance improves with scale, nor whether aggregate held-out pretraining loss predicts it.
Robustness to signature-extraction choices is examined, but the study does not fit scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test whether such laws bend.

reader_labels.reason: Perplexity-derived predictors show benchmark-performance fits and outperform the mean baseline in LOOCV; the held-out Qwen2.5-7B and Falcon-rw-7b tests also report low prediction MAEs (r1–r6, r13–r15).
